notes.front: What is an instrument proficiency check (IPC)?
notes.back: A check covering the Airman Certification Standards areas of operation for the rating held; it restores lapsed instrument currency.
notes.explanation: The regulation names it as the only way back once the instrument experience requirement has lapsed for more than six calendar months.
notes.example: Like a refresher assessment before rejoining a team after a long lay-off, but for instrument privileges: flown with an examiner or authorized instructor.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (d)(1)
notes.evidence: may reestablish instrument currency only by completing an instrument proficiency check. The instrument proficiency check must include the areas of operation contained in the applicable Airman Certification Standards
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is a safety pilot?
notes.back: The pilot in the other control seat during simulated instrument flight, holding at least a private pilot certificate for the aircraft's category and class.
notes.explanation: Someone must keep watch outside while the flying pilot sees only the instruments, so simulated instrument flight needs such a pilot in that seat; the rule's one other option is a sport pilot flight instructor giving solo cross-country endorsement training.
notes.example: Like a spotter in a gym: a friend with a private certificate keeps watch outside while you fly under a view-limiting hood.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.109 Flight instruction; Simulated instrument flight and certain flight tests (eCFR), paragraph (c)(1)
notes.evidence: The other control seat is occupied by a safety pilot who possesses at least: (i) A private pilot certificate with category and class ratings appropriate to the aircraft being flown
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which flight time may a pilot log as instrument time?
notes.back: Only the time spent operating the aircraft solely by reference to instruments, in actual or simulated instrument conditions.
notes.explanation: The rule limits logging to that flight time, not the whole flight.
notes.example: Like logging only the part of a drive spent in thick fog, not the whole journey.
notes.evidence: A person may log instrument time only for that flight time when the person operates the aircraft solely by reference to instruments under actual or simulated instrument flight conditions.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In an aeroplane, what must a pilot hold, besides the category and class rating, to act as pilot in command under IFR?
notes.back: An instrument rating on the pilot certificate (or an airline transport pilot certificate).
notes.explanation: Section 61.3(e) lists the instrument rating alongside category and class for airplanes, helicopters and powered-lift.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.3 Requirement for certificates, ratings, and authorizations (eCFR), paragraph (e)
notes.evidence: The appropriate aircraft category, class, type (if a class or type rating is required), and instrument rating on that person's pilot certificate for any airplane, helicopter, or powered-lift being flown
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What must an instructor certify before an instrument rating applicant takes the knowledge test?
notes.back: By a logbook or training record endorsement, that the applicant is prepared to take the knowledge test.
notes.explanation: The testing matrix also accepts a pilot school's ground-school graduation certificate instead.
notes.evidence: Receive a logbook or training record endorsement from an authorized instructor certifying that the person is prepared to take the required knowledge test
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: According to the FAA testing matrix, how many questions, how much time and what passing score does the Instrument Rating – Airplane knowledge test have?
notes.back: 60 questions, 2.0 hours, a passing score of 70.
notes.explanation: The matrix, dated September 2026, gives 2.0 hours; the Airman Certification Standards table still shows 2.5, and the matrix is followed here.
notes.source: FAA Airman Knowledge Testing Matrix (25 September 2026), Instrument Rating tests
notes.evidence: Instrument Rating Airplane 60 15 2.0 70
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How much cross-country time as pilot in command must an instrument-airplane applicant have logged, and how much of it in an aeroplane?
notes.back: 50 hours, of which 10 hours in an aeroplane.
notes.explanation: Section 61.65(d)(1) sets both figures; under 61.65(g) a combined private and instrument applicant may instead credit up to 45 hours flown performing pilot-in-command duties with an instructor.
notes.evidence: 50 hours of cross-country time as pilot in command, of which 10 hours must have been in an airplane
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How much actual or simulated instrument time must an instrument-airplane applicant log, and how much from an instructor?
notes.back: 40 hours, of which 15 from an authorized instructor holding an instrument-airplane rating.
notes.explanation: All 40 hours must be in the areas of operation listed in 61.65(c); the 15 instructor hours are part of them.
notes.evidence: Forty hours of actual or simulated instrument time in the areas of operation listed in paragraph (c) of this section, of which 15 hours must have been received from an authorized instructor who holds an instrument-airplane rating
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: The instrument time must include three hours of instrument training in an aeroplane from an authorized instructor within {{c1::2 calendar months}} before the practical test.
notes.back: 2 calendar months.
notes.explanation: Section 61.65(d)(2)(i) ties the three hours to the date of the practical test.
notes.evidence: Three hours of instrument flight training from an authorized instructor in an airplane that is appropriate to the instrument-airplane rating within 2 calendar months before the date of the practical test
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How long must the instrument-airplane training cross-country flight be?
notes.back: 250 nautical miles along airways or by ATC-directed routing.
notes.explanation: It is flown under IFR on a filed flight plan with an authorized instructor.
notes.evidence: (A) A flight of 250 nautical miles along airways or by directed routing from an air traffic control facility
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: On the instrument training cross-country, where must an instrument approach be flown?
notes.back: At each airport.
notes.explanation: Section 61.65(d)(2)(ii)(B) requires an approach at every airport on the flight.
notes.evidence: (B) An instrument approach at each airport; and (C) Three different kinds of approaches with the use of navigation systems.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: The instrument training cross-country must include {{c1::three}} different kinds of approaches using navigation systems.
notes.back: Three.
notes.explanation: The approaches must differ in kind, not just be three approaches.
notes.evidence: (C) Three different kinds of approaches with the use of navigation systems.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How much instrument time given by an instructor in a full flight simulator or flight training device may count, outside and inside a part 142 course?
notes.back: Up to 20 hours outside part 142; up to 30 hours under part 142.
notes.explanation: Section 61.65(h) sets the two limits by whether the time was completed under part 142.
notes.evidence: (1) A maximum of 30 hours may be performed in that full flight simulator or flight training device if the instrument time was completed in accordance with part 142 of this chapter
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How many hours of instrument time in a basic, and in an advanced, aviation training device may count toward the instrument rating?
notes.back: Up to 10 hours in a basic device; up to 20 hours in an advanced device.
notes.explanation: The device must be FAA-approved, the time given by an authorized instructor, and the training approved by the FAA.
notes.evidence: A maximum of 10 hours of instrument time received in a basic aviation training device or a maximum of 20 hours of instrument time received in an advanced aviation training device may be credited
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Outside a part 142 course, what is the most instrument time that simulators and training devices together may credit toward the rating?
notes.back: 20 hours in total.
notes.explanation: Section 61.65(j) caps any combination of devices, with only the part 142 exception.
notes.evidence: a person may not credit more than 20 total hours of instrument time in a full flight simulator, flight training device, aviation training device, or a combination
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: To act as pilot in command under IFR, a pilot must have performed and logged {{c1::six}} instrument approaches within the 6 calendar months preceding the month of the flight.
notes.back: Six.
notes.explanation: The approaches may be in actual weather or under simulated conditions using a view-limiting device.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (c)(1)
notes.evidence: Within the 6 calendar months preceding the month of the flight, that person performed and logged at least the following tasks and iterations
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Besides six approaches and intercepting and tracking courses, what else must the 61.57(c) instrument experience include?
notes.back: Holding procedures and tasks.
notes.explanation: It is one of the three items the rule lists for aircraft or device currency.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (c)(1)
notes.evidence: (i) Six instrument approaches. (ii) Holding procedures and tasks. (iii) Intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigational electronic systems.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Besides six approaches and holding, which navigation task completes the 61.57(c) instrument experience?
notes.back: Intercepting and tracking courses using navigational electronic systems.
notes.explanation: It is the third of the three listed items.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (c)(1)
notes.evidence: (iii) Intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigational electronic systems.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: May the instrument experience requirement be met in a flight simulator or training device?
notes.back: Yes: a full flight simulator, flight training device or aviation training device representing the aircraft category, in any combination with the aircraft.
notes.explanation: The device must represent the category whose instrument privileges are being kept, with the tasks flown in simulated instrument conditions.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (c)(2)
notes.evidence: A person may complete the instrument experience in any combination of an aircraft, full flight simulator, flight training device, or aviation training device.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: When does a pilot who is behind on instrument experience need an IPC rather than simply flying the tasks again?
notes.back: Once the experience requirement has lapsed for more than six calendar months.
notes.explanation: Within that period the pilot may still catch up; after it, the IPC is the only route back.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (d)(1)
notes.evidence: a person who has failed to meet the instrument experience requirements of paragraph (c) of this section for more than six calendar months may reestablish instrument currency only by completing an instrument proficiency check
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: For an aeroplane pilot, in what may an IPC be flown?
notes.back: In an aircraft of the right category, or a full flight simulator or flight training device representing that category.
notes.explanation: Section 61.57(d)(2) lists only these for other than gliders; an aviation training device is not among them.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (d)(2)
notes.evidence: (i) In an aircraft that is appropriate to the aircraft category; (ii) For other than a glider, in a full flight simulator or flight training device that is representative of the aircraft category
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: When may an authorized instructor log instrument time without flying solely by instruments?
notes.back: When conducting instrument flight instruction in actual instrument flight conditions.
notes.explanation: Section 61.51(g)(2) grants this to the instructor, not to a safety pilot.
notes.evidence: An authorized instructor may log instrument time when conducting instrument flight instruction in actual instrument flight conditions.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: For each instrument approach logged toward currency, what must the logbook record about the approach itself?
notes.back: Its location and its type.
notes.explanation: Section 61.51(g)(3) requires these for time logged to meet 61.57(c).
notes.evidence: (i) The location and type of each instrument approach accomplished; and (ii) The name of the safety pilot, if required.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Logging simulated instrument time toward currency, whose name must the logbook record when one was required?
notes.back: The safety pilot's.
notes.explanation: It is the second item that 61.51(g)(3) requires for currency logging.
notes.evidence: (ii) The name of the safety pilot, if required.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What vision must a safety pilot have?
notes.back: Adequate vision forward and to each side, unless a competent observer on board adequately supplements it.
notes.explanation: Section 91.109(c)(2) accepts an observer as a supplement.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.109 Flight instruction; Simulated instrument flight and certain flight tests (eCFR), paragraph (c)(2)
notes.evidence: The safety pilot has adequate vision forward and to each side of the aircraft, or a competent observer in the aircraft adequately supplements the vision of the safety pilot
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A pilot with single- and multiengine class ratings takes the instrument practical test in a single-engine aeroplane. What limitation is issued?
notes.back: “Multiengine Limited to VFR Only.”
notes.explanation: Taking the test in a multiengine aeroplane instead confers instrument privileges for the single-engine rating automatically.
notes.source: Instrument Rating – Airplane Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-8C), knowledge test and practical test eligibility
notes.evidence: takes the instrument rating practical test in a single-engine airplane, the certificate issued must bear the limitation “Multiengine Limited to VFR Only.”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A private pilot with no instrument rating plans a visual departure, but the destination is forecast to be below VFR minimums on arrival. May the pilot act as pilot in command into it?
notes.back: C) No.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if no IFR clearance is requested
B) Yes, with a safety pilot aboard
C) No
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rule applies to weather below VFR minimums, not only to IFR flights. B: a safety pilot serves simulated instrument flight and does not supply an instrument rating.
notes.explanation: Section 61.3(e) bars acting as pilot in command in weather below VFR minimums without an instrument rating.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.3 Requirement for certificates, ratings, and authorizations (eCFR), paragraph (e)
notes.evidence: No person may act as pilot in command of a civil aircraft under IFR or in weather conditions less than the minimums prescribed for VFR flight unless that person holds
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: An applicant has 38 hours of simulated instrument time, 16 of them with an instructor holding an instrument-airplane rating. Is the 40-hour requirement met?
notes.back: A) No, two more hours are needed.
notes.choices:
A) No, two more hours are needed
B) Yes, because 15 instructor hours are met
C) No, 40 instructor hours are needed
notes.choicesExplained: B: the 15 instructor hours are part of the 40, not a replacement for them. C: only 15 of the 40 must come from an instructor.
notes.explanation: Both figures in 61.65(d)(2) must be met: 40 hours in total, 15 of them from an instructor.
notes.evidence: Forty hours of actual or simulated instrument time in the areas of operation listed in paragraph (c) of this section, of which 15 hours must have been received from an authorized instructor
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A private pilot has 60 hours of cross-country pilot-in-command time, all flown in helicopters and none in aeroplanes. Does this meet the instrument-airplane cross-country requirement?
notes.back: A) No, 10 of the hours must be in an aeroplane.
notes.choices:
A) No, 10 of the hours must be in an aeroplane
B) Yes, 60 exceeds 50
C) Yes, category does not matter
notes.choicesExplained: B: the total is met but the aeroplane part is not. C: the rule names aeroplane time specifically.
notes.explanation: Section 61.65(d)(1) requires 10 of the 50 hours in an airplane.
notes.evidence: 50 hours of cross-country time as pilot in command, of which 10 hours must have been in an airplane
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: An applicant flew three hours of instrument training in an aeroplane with an instructor in May and schedules the practical test for November. Do those hours meet the three-hour requirement?
notes.back: C) No, they fall outside 2 calendar months before the test.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, any three instructor hours count
B) Yes, if they were logged within 6 calendar months
C) No, they fall outside 2 calendar months before the test
notes.choicesExplained: A: these three hours must fall in a set window. B: six calendar months is the currency period, not this window.
notes.explanation: The three hours must fall within 2 calendar months before the practical test.
notes.evidence: within 2 calendar months before the date of the practical test
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: With an instructor under IFR, a student flies 180 NM on airways to two airports, flying an approach at each. Does this meet the training cross-country requirement?
notes.back: B) No.
notes.choices:
A) Yes
B) No
C) Yes, if a third approach is flown at home
notes.choicesExplained: A: the flight is too short and has too few approach kinds. C: the distance is still short of 250 NM.
notes.explanation: The flight must cover 250 NM and include three different kinds of approaches.
notes.evidence: (A) A flight of 250 nautical miles along airways or by directed routing from an air traffic control facility; (B) An instrument approach at each airport; and (C) Three different kinds of approaches
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A pilot logged six approaches, holding and course tracking in March 2026 and nothing since. May the pilot act as pilot in command under IFR on 20 September 2026?
notes.back: A) Yes.
notes.choices:
A) Yes
B) No, the tasks are more than six months old
C) No, an IPC is needed
notes.choicesExplained: B: the window counts the 6 calendar months before September, which include March. C: an IPC is needed only after more than six further calendar months without currency.
notes.explanation: For a September flight, the preceding 6 calendar months run from March to August.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (c)(1)
notes.evidence: Within the 6 calendar months preceding the month of the flight, that person performed and logged at least the following tasks and iterations
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: The same pilot, current from tasks flown in March 2026, wants to file IFR on 5 October 2026. What is the position?
notes.back: C) Not current, but may regain currency by flying the tasks.
notes.choices:
A) Current until the end of March 2027
B) Not current, and only an IPC will do
C) Not current, but may regain currency by flying the tasks, for example with a safety pilot
notes.choicesExplained: A: the tasks no longer fall in the 6 calendar months before October. B: the IPC is required only after more than six calendar months of lapse.
notes.explanation: For an October flight the window is April to September; the IPC rule applies only after a lapse of more than six calendar months.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (d)(1)
notes.evidence: a person who has failed to meet the instrument experience requirements of paragraph (c) of this section for more than six calendar months may reestablish instrument currency only by completing an instrument proficiency check
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A pilot last met the instrument experience requirement in 2024 and has not flown under the hood since. How can the pilot regain instrument currency?
notes.back: A) Only by an IPC.
notes.choices:
A) Only by an IPC
B) By logging six approaches, holding and tracking with a safety pilot
C) By a flight review
notes.choicesExplained: B: flying the tasks again works only within the first six calendar months of lapse. C: a flight review does not restore instrument currency.
notes.explanation: After more than six calendar months of lapse, the IPC is the only route.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (d)(1)
notes.evidence: may reestablish instrument currency only by completing an instrument proficiency check
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A pilot needs an IPC and asks a local authorized instructor, who is not an examiner and works for no airline. May the instructor give it?
notes.back: A) Yes.
notes.choices:
A) Yes
B) No, only an examiner may
C) No, only a company check pilot may
notes.choicesExplained: B: examiners are one of several listed people. C: company check pilots are also listed, but only for their own operator's employees.
notes.explanation: An authorized instructor is on the 61.57(d)(3) list.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 61.57 Recent flight experience: Pilot in command (eCFR), paragraph (d)(3)
notes.evidence: (iv) An authorized instructor; or (v) A person approved by the Administrator to conduct instrument practical tests.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: On a 1.4-hour flight, a pilot spends 0.6 hours in cloud flying solely by instruments. How much instrument time may be logged?
notes.back: C) 0.6 hours.
notes.choices:
A) 1.4 hours
B) None, unless an instructor is aboard
C) 0.6 hours
notes.choicesExplained: A: only the time flown solely by instruments counts. B: the pilot flying by instruments logs it; an instructor is not needed.
notes.explanation: Instrument time is only the flight time spent solely by reference to instruments.
notes.evidence: A person may log instrument time only for that flight time when the person operates the aircraft solely by reference to instruments
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: After a hood session, a pilot logs “3 approaches, 1.1 simulated instrument”. What is missing for currency purposes?
notes.back: B) Each approach's location and type, and the safety pilot's name.
notes.choices:
A) The instructor's certificate number
B) Each approach's location and type, and the safety pilot's name
C) Nothing
notes.choicesExplained: A: 61.51(g)(3) does not ask for this. C: the entry lacks the items the rule lists.
notes.explanation: Section 61.51(g)(3) lists these items for time logged toward 61.57(c).
notes.evidence: (i) The location and type of each instrument approach accomplished; and (ii) The name of the safety pilot, if required.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A friend who holds only a student pilot certificate offers to be safety pilot for your hood practice in a four-seat single-engine aeroplane. Can they?
notes.back: A) No.
notes.choices:
A) No
B) Yes, if they have good vision to each side
C) Yes, if the aeroplane has dual controls
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: vision and dual controls are also required, but the safety pilot must first hold at least a private pilot certificate for the category and class (the sport pilot instructor case aside).
notes.explanation: Section 91.109(c)(1) sets the private pilot certificate as the minimum for this aeroplane.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.109 Flight instruction; Simulated instrument flight and certain flight tests (eCFR), paragraph (c)(1)
notes.evidence: The other control seat is occupied by a safety pilot who possesses at least: (i) A private pilot certificate with category and class ratings appropriate to the aircraft being flown
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: An applicant flew 25 hours of approved instrument training in an advanced aviation training device, all with an instructor. How many count toward the rating?
notes.choicesExplained: A: the advanced-device limit is 20. B: 10 is the limit for a basic device.
notes.explanation: The advanced-device limit is 20 hours, which is also the overall device cap outside part 142.
notes.evidence: a maximum of 20 hours of instrument time received in an advanced aviation training device may be credited
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under Pilot Qualifications, the Instrument Rating standards first list a risk that sets being skilled against being legally current. What is it called?
notes.back: “Proficiency versus currency”.
notes.explanation: The Instrument Rating standards list it first among the risks an applicant must identify, assess and mitigate for pilot qualifications.
notes.source: Instrument Rating – Airplane Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-8C), Area of Operation I, Task A, Pilot Qualifications
notes.evidence: mitigate risk associated with: IR.I.A.R1 Proficiency versus currency. IR.I.A.R2 Personal minimums.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How long is the instrument training cross-country for an aeroplane rating compared with a helicopter rating?
notes.back: 250 NM for aeroplanes; 100 NM for helicopters.
notes.explanation: Both must still include an approach at each airport and three different kinds of approaches.
notes.evidence: (A) A flight of 100 nautical miles along airways or by directed routing from an air traffic control facility
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force
